nameStory: The "eastern" part is simple geography - this newt lives in the eastern half of North America. The word "newt" comes from the Middle English "ewte," which evolved from "an ewte" being misheard as "a newte" over centuries of spoken language. It's related to the Old English "efte," which gives us the name for the bright orange juvenile stage called a "red eft."
description: The eastern newt is a small salamander that lives a fascinating double life - part on land, part in water. Adults are olive green with small red spots and grow up to 5 inches long. But their babies are completely different: bright orange "red efts" that live on land for several years before returning to water. These common amphibians are found throughout New England's ponds, lakes, and slow streams.

idTips.label: Color/Pattern
idTips.description: Adults are olive to yellowish-green with a row of red spots circled in black along each side - like tiny bull's-eyes dotting their flanks

idTips.label: Skin
idTips.description: Adult skin feels smooth and slightly slimy when wet, but becomes rougher and more granular during their brief land phases

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Adults reach 3-5 inches long - about the length of your index finger - with a flattened tail that's taller than it is wide

idTips.label: Eyes
idTips.description: Large, dark eyes that seem oversized for their head, giving them an alert, almost cartoon-like expression

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Found in shallow, weedy areas of ponds and slow streams where they can easily surface to breathe - often visible swimming just below the surface

habitat: Eastern newts love quiet, shallow waters with plenty of vegetation - think weedy pond edges, slow-moving streams, and woodland pools. They prefer waters with muddy or leafy bottoms where they can hunt for small prey. During their red eft stage, you'll find them under logs, rocks, and leaf litter in moist forests near these water bodies.

seasonality.spring: Adults become active in warming waters and begin breeding. Look for them swimming in shallow areas of ponds and streams as ice melts.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity time - adults are easily spotted swimming and hunting in ponds. Bright orange red efts wander forest floors, especially after rain.
seasonality.fall: Adults prepare for winter by moving to deeper water. Young efts continue their land phase, often found under logs and rocks.
seasonality.winter: Adults overwinter underwater, sometimes visible moving slowly beneath ice. Red efts hibernate under logs, rocks, and deep leaf litter.

funFact: Eastern newts are living poison factories - their skin produces tetrodotoxin, the same deadly toxin found in pufferfish, making them completely inedible to fish and explaining why that bright orange red eft can boldly wander around in broad daylight without fear.
confusionNotes: Adult newts might be confused with other small salamanders, but those red spots circled in black are unique - no other New England salamander has this bull's-eye pattern. Red efts are unmistakable with their bright orange color, but remember that other juvenile salamanders are typically brown or gray.
contextualKnowledge: The eastern newt is actually the only newt species found in New England - all other local salamanders belong to different families. Many people use "salamander" and "newt" interchangeably, but newts are just one special group of salamanders that return to water as adults.
compareHints: Since the eastern newt is the only member of its genus in New England, compare it to other salamander families. Unlike lungless salamanders (like red-backed salamanders), newts have lungs and must surface to breathe when in water. Unlike mole salamanders, adult newts are aquatic rather than terrestrial, and they lack the robust, chunky build of species like spotted salamanders.
